video_title: Design Patterns Are About Forces, Not Code Templates
core_insight: A design pattern is Context + Forces → Solution with Consequences. It names recurring trade-offs so teams can make change cheap in a specific dimension, not a code template to copy.

scenes.voice: Why do teams keep reinventing the same solution with different names?
scenes.visual: Three sticky notes appear: payment processing, pricing rules, UI events. Same shape, different labels.

scenes.voice: The real problem isn't coding skill. It's repeatability under change and communication across teams.
scenes.visual: Two developers draw different diagrams for the same requirement. Inconsistency highlights.

scenes.voice: Obvious approach is inline conditionals and copy-paste. It works once. Then every new provider, rule, or event forces edits in core code.
scenes.visual: Code block with growing if-else chain. Red warning on core order flow.

scenes.voice: The constraint is what varies versus what stays stable, and who creates objects versus who uses them.
scenes.visual: Split screen: Varies vs Stable. Arrows to Creator vs User.

scenes.voice: Patterns name those forces. Strategy for interchangeable algorithms. Factory or DI for constrained construction. Observer or Event for loose communication. Adapter for incompatible contracts.
scenes.visual: Simple mapping from forces to pattern families.
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    RequirementChange[Changing requirement] --> Forces[Forces: flexibility vs complexity]
    Forces --> Decision{Choose structure}
    Decision -->|Vary algorithm| Strategy[Strategy]
    Decision -->|Vary construction| Factory[Factory/DI]
    Decision -->|Vary communication| Observer[Observer/Event]
    Strategy --> Tradeoffs[More indirection, better testability]
    Factory --> Tradeoffs
    Observer --> Tradeoffs

scenes.voice: You pay for it. Patterns add indirection, readability cost, and cognitive load. Premature generality creates dead abstractions.
scenes.visual: Scale balancing Flexibility vs Indirection. Red X on premature pattern.

scenes.voice: So use a pattern only after you can name the forces. Choose to make a specific kind of change cheap, not to be clever.
scenes.visual: Enterprise payment example: Strategy for providers, Factory for creation, Adapter for normalization. Order flow unchanged.

scenes.voice: Patterns are architectural shorthand for trade-offs. Learn forces first.

mental_model: Context + Forces → Solution with Consequences. Identify what varies and what is stable, list forces like flexibility vs complexity and decoupling vs indirection, then pick a pattern family to make a specific change cheap and accept the indirection cost.
final_takeaway: Patterns name forces, not code. Pay for indirection only when the forces exist.
